z-m-11-01.title: The total is bigger than the number of students. Is the table wrong?
z-m-11-01.topic: Table totals and the number of people surveyed (data where one person marked more than once)
z-m-11-01.goal: When the total in a table differs from the number of students surveyed, don't conclude the table is wrong, but say what else you need to know such as the survey method, and fix your judgment with new information.
z-m-11-01.material:
Class 3 of Grade 4 has 28 students. They surveyed 'the place they want to go for a field trip' and made the table below. The numbers in the table are the number of students who put a ○ for that place.

| Place | Museum | Zoo | Science center | Amusement park | Total |
| Students (number of people) | 12 | 10 | 9 | 7 | 38 |

Jia said, "The total is 38 but our class has 28 students. The table is wrong!" (The table is written in words, so there is no picture. The rows of the table are, from the top, place and number of students.)
z-m-11-01.thinking.0: Telling apart what the table alone can and can't tell you
z-m-11-01.thinking.1: Saying for yourself what more information is needed
z-m-11-01.thinking.2: Fixing your judgment and confidence each time new information comes out
z-m-11-01.prereq.0: Reading the number for each item in a table and adding (Grades 3-4 level)
z-m-11-01.prereq.1: That in a survey there are cases where 'one person chooses only one thing' and cases where 'one person chooses several things'
z-m-11-01.s.s1.prompt: More data is revealed one piece at a time. Choose your thinking each time.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write the total and the number of students side by side and first look at how different they are.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.hint.1: Using a small example (3 students), count how many more marks than students there are when one person marks two places.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.info: What is known now is only the table and the number of students (28). The survey sheet hasn't been seen yet.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: Do you think this table is wrong?
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.after: The total of 38 could be because of the survey method, or because the same student was counted twice while counting. You can only know by looking at the survey sheet.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The total differs from the number of students, so the table was counted wrongly
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You blamed the way of counting just because the total differs from the number of students. First think about whether this could happen depending on the survey method.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Until we see the survey sheet, we can't know whether the table is wrong
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You stopped in the right place. This is thinking that remembered that with the same table, the total can differ depending on the survey method.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: If the total is bigger than the number of students, the table is always right
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: On the contrary, you believed it too fast. The reason the total is big could be a counting mistake, so you need to check.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.1.info: The survey sheet said, 'Put a ○ on the places you want to go. You may choose up to two places.' All 28 students put a ○ on at least one place.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: How many students put a ○ on two places?
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.1.after: If everyone marked at least one place and at most two, the number of marks, 38, is the number of students, 28, plus the number of students who chose two places. So 10 students chose two places.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You did well to find that the amount you get by subtracting the number of students, 28, from the number of ○ marks, 38, is the number of marks made 'one more time'.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: It looks like you thought of half of 28. Think about what the difference between the 38 marks and the 28 students means.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: It looks like you thought of half of 38. Count how many more marks than students there are if one person chose two places.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.2.info: The teacher checked again, and 4 students didn't put a ○ on any place. The other 24 students put a ○ on one or two places.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now, how many students put a ○ on two places?
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.2.after: Among the 24 students, if 10 chose only one place and 14 chose two places, the number of marks is 10+28=38. When new information comes in, the answer changes even with the same table.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You mixed up the number of students who marked no place and the number of students who marked two places. Those are different people.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You carried over the answer from the earlier step as it was. Check again whether the 4 students you just learned about need to go into the calculation.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is thinking that worked it out again with the new information. You found the case where the 24 students choose one or two places and the number of marks becomes 38.
z-m-11-01.s.s1.reflect: At first, was your thought closer to 'the table is wrong' or 'we can't tell'? What did the survey sheet and the information about the 4 students who didn't answer each change? If there is still something you don't know, what is it?
z-m-11-01.s.s2.prompt: You know that the survey sheet said 'up to two places'. Choose all the things you can safely say using only the numbers in this table and what's on the survey sheet.
z-m-11-01.s.s2.hint.0: Imagine one student who put a ○ on two places, the museum and the zoo. Which boxes does that student go into?
z-m-11-01.s.s2.hint.1: In each statement, look at whether 'the same student could be counted twice'.
z-m-11-01.s.s2.o.a: The students who chose the museum or the zoo total 22
z-m-11-01.s.s2.r.a: 12+10=22 may be a value that counted a student who chose both places twice. You can say it is 22 students 'or fewer', but you can't say for sure it is 22.
z-m-11-01.s.s2.o.b: The students who chose the museum are 12
z-m-11-01.s.s2.r.b: One box of the table is the number of students who put a ○ on that place, so you can read it this way.
z-m-11-01.s.s2.o.c: 38, the sum of the four numbers in the table, is the number of students who put a ○
z-m-11-01.s.s2.r.c: 38 is the number of times ○ was marked. One student may have marked twice, so you must not read it as the number of students.
z-m-11-01.s.s2.o.d: The 12 students who chose the museum and the 10 students who chose the zoo are different students
z-m-11-01.s.s2.r.d: You could choose two places, so the same student could be in both groups.
z-m-11-01.s.s2.o.e: The students who chose the science center are 2 more than the students who chose the amusement park
z-m-11-01.s.s2.r.e: Each box is the number of students who chose that place, so a statement that compares two boxes is safe.
z-m-11-01.s.s2.explain: The number in one box is the number of students who chose that place, so a statement that reads one box or compares two boxes is safe. A value that adds up the boxes may have counted the same student several times, so you can't read it as the 'number of students'.
z-m-11-01.s.s3.prompt: Jia said, "The total is bigger than the number of students, so the table is wrong!" What would you say to Jia? Also write what else you need to know to decide whether the table is wrong.
z-m-11-01.s.s3.hint.0: Think about how the survey would have had to be done for the total of the table to equal the number of students.
z-m-11-01.s.s3.hint.1: Write at least one possible reason the total is bigger, and match each one with what you would need to look at to check it.
z-m-11-01.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., Even if the total is big, I need to know ...
z-m-11-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you avoid saying the table is wrong, and say at least one case where the total can be bigger?
z-m-11-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write concretely 'what else you need to know'?
z-m-11-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Does what you wrote sound like checking together, without making Jia feel wrong?
z-m-11-01.s.s3.model.0: A big total doesn't mean it's wrong right away. If the survey let each person put a ○ on two or more places, the total can be bigger than the number of students. Let's first check on the survey sheet how many places you could choose.
z-m-11-01.s.s3.model.1: We don't know yet whether the table is wrong. Students from another class may have answered too, or the same student may have been counted twice, so we have to check who answered and how they were counted.
z-m-11-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: It also said to check, besides multiple answers, the range of people who answered and the way of counting.

z-m-11-02.title: Minseo's way of reading the pictograph: what looks strange?
z-m-11-02.topic: What the big picture and the small picture stand for in a pictograph
z-m-11-02.goal: Show with a counterexample that in a pictograph where pictures of different sizes have different values, comparing by only counting pictures can be wrong, and state the conditions under which comparing by counting is fine.
z-m-11-02.material:
The number of breads sold in a day at four neighborhood bakeries is shown in a pictograph. One big bread picture stands for 10 breads, and one small bread picture stands for 1 bread. There is no picture, so it is written in words.

| Bakery | Big bread pictures | Small bread pictures |
| 가 | 3 | 4 |
| 나 | 2 | 9 |
| 다 | 4 | 0 |
| 라 | 3 | 7 |

Minseo read this graph and summed it up in the six lines below.
z-m-11-02.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in a solution
z-m-11-02.thinking.1: Testing a claim with a counterexample
z-m-11-02.thinking.2: Stating the conditions under which it holds
z-m-11-02.prereq.0: Reading the numbers that one big picture and one small picture stand for and writing them as tens and ones (Grade 3 pictograph level)
z-m-11-02.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of two numbers
z-m-11-02.s.s1.prompt: Which line of Minseo's summary is strange? (Line numbers start from 1.)
z-m-11-02.s.s1.hint.0: To check what line 6 says, find the number of breads sold by the bakery with the most pictures and the bakery with the fewest pictures, and put them side by side.
z-m-11-02.s.s1.hint.1: Put the numbers sold that you found in lines 2 to 4 in order of size again, and compare them with the conclusion of line 6.
z-m-11-02.s.s1.line.0: 1. One big bread picture stands for 10 breads, and one small bread picture stands for 1 bread.
z-m-11-02.s.s1.line.1: 2. Bakery 가 has 3 big pictures and 4 small pictures, so it sold 30+4=34 breads.
z-m-11-02.s.s1.line.2: 3. Bakery 나 has 2 big pictures and 9 small pictures, so it sold 20+9=29 breads.
z-m-11-02.s.s1.line.3: 4. Bakery 다 has only 4 big pictures, so it sold 40 breads. Bakery 라 has 3 big pictures and 7 small pictures, so it sold 37 breads.
z-m-11-02.s.s1.line.4: 5. The number of pictures for the four bakeries is 가 7, 나 11, 다 4, 라 10.
z-m-11-02.s.s1.line.5: 6. The bakery with the most pictures is Bakery 나 (11), so Bakery 나 sold the most bread.
z-m-11-02.s.s1.explain: Line 6 is strange. In this graph, pictures of different sizes stand for different numbers, so having more pictures doesn't mean selling more. Bakery 나 has 11 pictures but sold 29, and Bakery 다 has only 4 pictures but, because they are big pictures, sold 40, the most.
z-m-11-02.s.s2.prompt: In this graph, comparing by counting the number of pictures could be wrong. Choose all the cases in which you can say which side has more by looking only at the number of pictures.
z-m-11-02.s.s2.hint.0: Take Bakery 가 (big 3, small 4) and Bakery 나 (big 2, small 9), and compare the number of big pictures and the number of small pictures separately.
z-m-11-02.s.s2.hint.1: For each choice, make one example and test whether the side with more pictures must also have sold more.
z-m-11-02.s.s2.o.a: A case where both bakeries use only big bread pictures
z-m-11-02.s.s2.r.a: If there is only one size of picture, one picture stands for the same number, so comparing only the number of pictures is fine.
z-m-11-02.s.s2.o.b: A case where the difference in the number of pictures is very big, like 11 and 4
z-m-11-02.s.s2.r.b: You thought a big difference would be safe. Look at 나 and 다 in this graph: even with a big difference, it flipped.
z-m-11-02.s.s2.o.c: A case where one bakery has more big pictures and more small pictures than the other
z-m-11-02.s.s2.r.c: You found that if it has more of both the big and the small pictures, the total has to be bigger too.
z-m-11-02.s.s2.o.d: A case where both bakeries use a mix of big and small pictures
z-m-11-02.s.s2.r.d: Being mixed alone doesn't let you compare. You have to look separately at how many big pictures and how many small pictures there are.
z-m-11-02.s.s2.explain: If there is only one size of picture, or if one side has more big pictures and more small pictures, you can judge by the number of pictures alone. If sizes are mixed and one side has more big pictures while the other has more small pictures, you have to find the values and compare.
z-m-11-02.s.s3.prompt: Explain to Minseo, using numbers, why the statement in line 6 doesn't fit this graph. (Write the number of pictures and the number sold for two bakeries.)
z-m-11-02.s.s3.hint.0: Find the number of pictures and the number sold for Bakery 다 and Bakery 나, and write them in two lines.
z-m-11-02.s.s3.hint.1: First write in one sentence how the bigger or smaller number of pictures and the bigger or smaller number sold differ in the two bakeries.
z-m-11-02.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., Bakery 나 has ... pictures but ...
z-m-11-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate to check that the number of pictures and the number sold for the two bakeries you gave match each other?
z-m-11-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say why "more pictures ≠ sold more" happens (the pictures stand for different numbers)?
z-m-11-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: If you added a case where comparing by the number of pictures is fine, did you check that this case really holds?
z-m-11-02.s.s3.model.0: Bakery 나 has the most pictures with 11, but it has only 2 big pictures, so it is 20+9=29. Bakery 다 has only 4 pictures, but they are all big pictures, so it is 40. Pictures stand for different numbers depending on size, so you must not just count the pictures.
z-m-11-02.s.s3.model.1: One big picture is 10 and one small picture is 1, so you don't add by the number of pictures; you add big pictures by 10 and small pictures by 1. Then Bakery 가 is 34 and Bakery 라 is 37, and the pictures are 7 and 10, so the order is the same but the difference is different.
z-m-11-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: It also gave an example where the order is the same, to tell it apart from a case that is right by chance.

z-m-11-03.title: Milk carton bar graph: how much should one scale mark be?
z-m-11-03.topic: Deciding the size of one mark on the vertical scale of a bar graph
z-m-11-03.goal: Find different ways to decide the size of one vertical scale mark so that the data values land exactly on scale lines and fit on the paper, and say that each way is easier to read in a different respect.
z-m-11-03.material:
We want to show the number of milk cartons collected by four groups of Grade 4 at our school in a bar graph.

| Group | Sun | Moon | Star | Forest |
| Milk cartons (number) | 24 | 36 | 60 | 48 |

The rules of the graph paper:
- The vertical scale starts at 0 and goes up. Call the number of cartons that one scale line stands for u (a natural number), and the number of vertical scale marks n.
- Because of the paper size, n is 5 or more and 12 or fewer.
- The biggest value (60) must fit inside the graph. That is, the top scale must be 60 or more.
- The end of each bar must sit exactly on a scale line so that the value can be read exactly.
z-m-11-03.thinking.0: Finding several designs that satisfy the conditions
z-m-11-03.thinking.1: Finding the problem in a plan that breaks the conditions
z-m-11-03.thinking.2: Comparing the pros and cons of designs
z-m-11-03.prereq.0: Reading the scale of a bar graph and drawing bars (Grade 3 level)
z-m-11-03.prereq.1: Experience with multiplication facts and division (Grades 3-4 level)
z-m-11-03.s.s1.prompt: Minho said he will make one mark 10 cartons and draw 6 vertical marks. (The top scale is 60.) What is the problem with this plan?
z-m-11-03.s.s1.hint.0: Check the conditions written in the rules one by one against Minho's plan (10, 6 marks).
z-m-11-03.s.s1.hint.1: Check one by one whether 24, 36, and 48 sit on scale lines that go up by 10.
z-m-11-03.s.s1.o.a: The longest bar (60) goes out of the paper and doesn't fit in the graph
z-m-11-03.s.s1.r.a: 10×6=60, so 60 touches the top scale exactly. You can find that out by checking the plan with numbers.
z-m-11-03.s.s1.o.b: The scale doesn't start at 0, so you can't read values from the bar heights
z-m-11-03.s.s1.r.b: This plan starts at 0 too. Check the plan against the conditions in the rules one by one.
z-m-11-03.s.s1.o.c: There are only 6 vertical marks, so the number of marks is too few compared with the rules
z-m-11-03.s.s1.r.c: The rules say the number of marks only has to be 5 or more. 6 marks is within the condition.
z-m-11-03.s.s1.o.d: The ends of the 24, 36, and 48 bars sit between scale lines
z-m-11-03.s.s1.r.d: You found it right. If the scale is 10, 20, 30, ..., then 24 sits between 20 and 30.
z-m-11-03.s.s1.explain: 10×6=60, so it fits on the paper and the number of marks is within the condition, but 24 sits between 20 and 30, 36 between 30 and 40, and 48 between 40 and 50. So they don't sit exactly on scale lines.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 scale plans that satisfy all the rules, with different scale sizes. (The number of cartons per mark u and the number of vertical marks n. If the scale size u is different, count it as a different plan.)
z-m-11-03.s.s2.hint.0: Decide the size of one mark, and check whether 24, 36, 48, and 60 each sit exactly on the scale lines that go up by that size. If any value sits between scale lines, that size won't work.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.hint.1: If you find a size where all four values sit on scale lines, count how many marks you need to reach 60 and check that it is within the condition on the number of marks.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.ok.c1: u is a natural number and n is from 5 to 12.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.fail.c1: u must be a natural number and n must be from 5 to 12.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The top scale is 60 or more, so the 60 bar fits.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The top scale (u×n) is less than 60, so the longest bar goes out of the paper.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The ends of all four bars sit exactly on scale lines.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The end of some bar sits between scale lines, so it is hard to read the value exactly.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.explain: With u=6, n=10, the bar ends sit exactly at 4 marks, 6 marks, 10 marks, and 8 marks. With u=12, n=5, they are 2 marks, 3 marks, 5 marks, and 4 marks. u=4 doesn't work because you would need more than 12 marks to reach 60, and u=3 or 2 don't work because they need even more marks.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one of the two plans you made, and write what is easy to read or a drawback for this data, using numbers. (For example, how the difference in bar heights between groups looks.)
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: In the two plans, count how many marks the difference in height is between the Sun group (24) and Moon group (36) bars.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare the plan with many scale lines and the plan with few, and see which makes it more comfortable to read values.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g., If one mark is ... cartons, ...
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check again that the scale and number of marks in your plan keep the rules (60 fits and values sit exactly on scale lines)?
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Is the advantage you mentioned something that can be checked with numbers, like the difference in bar heights?
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you also think of situations where the other plan is better?
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.model.0: I like the plan where one mark is 6 cartons. The Sun group is 4 marks and the Moon group is 6 marks, so there's a difference of 2 marks between the two groups, which makes it easy to compare by eye.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.model.1: If one mark is 12 cartons, there are only 5 marks, so the graph fits on a small paper and looks neat. But the Sun group (2 marks) and the Moon group (3 marks) differ by only 1 mark, so the difference looks small.
z-m-11-03.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: It mentioned both the advantage and the drawback.

z-m-11-04.title: Why are the results different between a show of hands and a slip vote?
z-m-11-04.topic: How the survey method (show of hands, slip vote) affects the result
z-m-11-04.goal: Check with data that with the same class, a different survey method can give a different result, and rewrite what you can say and how sure you can be each time new data comes in.
z-m-11-04.material: Class 2 of Grade 4 has 24 students. They want to decide a game to play together at break time. The candidates are dodgeball, board games, and jump rope, and each person votes for only one. Half of 24 is 12.
z-m-11-04.thinking.0: Comparing two sets of data from different methods
z-m-11-04.thinking.1: Adjusting the range of what you say when new data comes in
z-m-11-04.thinking.2: Writing a sentence that reports the result along with its conditions
z-m-11-04.prereq.0: Reading vote results in a table and finding the total
z-m-11-04.prereq.1: Knowing what half of the whole is (half of 24 is 12)
z-m-11-04.prereq.2: Comparing the sizes of two numbers
z-m-11-04.s.s1.prompt: The vote results are revealed step by step. At each step, choose what you can say.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.hint.0: Put the numbers for dodgeball, board games, and jump rope in the two votes side by side, and compare each with 12 (half).
z-m-11-04.s.s1.hint.1: Look separately at whether the order (who is first) is the same and whether the size (how many people) is the same.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.info: On the first day, everyone kept their eyes open and raised a hand for one choice. The results are dodgeball 14, board games 6, and jump rope 4 (24 in total). When raising hands, the other friends could see each other raising their hands.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: What can you say from this result?
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.after: You have to tell apart the fact within this vote (14) from guesses about the students' real feelings. Both kinds of statements are fitting at this step.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The students who chose dodgeball in the show of hands were 14, more than 12, so you can say that in this vote it is more than half
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You told the result of the vote as it is and added the range "in this vote".
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: The show-of-hands method can't be trusted, so you can't say anything with this result
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Even if the method has flaws, it's data in which all 24 took part. Throwing it out as nothing is too much.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: They could see each other, so some students may have raised hands to follow, so we need to check more whether dodgeball is really popular
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You thought about the fact that the method can affect the result, and adjusted how sure you are.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.info: The next day they voted again with slips without names. The results are dodgeball 10, board games 8, and jump rope 6 (24 in total).
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: How should we say "dodgeball has the most" and "more than half chose dodgeball"?
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.after: Dodgeball had the most both times. But whether it went over half (12) changed with the method. How sure you can be depends on "what" you say.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Both statements can be said as they are. The first-day vote is more trustworthy because the number of people is the same
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: 24 people voted both times. The number of people being the same is not a reason that the first day is more trustworthy.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: "Has the most" can be said both times, but "more than half" doesn't hold in the slip vote, so we say it carefully
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You put the two results side by side and checked in which vote each statement holds.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The results were different, so the votes can't be trusted and we can't even say dodgeball has the most
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Dodgeball had the most both times. What changed was the size, not the order.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Slips probably made people care less about what others thought, so I trust the slip result more and say only up to "dodgeball has the most"
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You decided which result to trust more based on the difference in methods, and narrowed the range of what you say.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.info: They say only 4 students changed their minds between the two times. 2 changed from dodgeball to board games, 2 changed from dodgeball to jump rope, and the other 20 made the same choice both times.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: If this story is true, what thought is fitting?
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.after: To get over 12 from dodgeball's 10, 3 or more of the 4 who changed would have to be added (2 would make 12, equal to half). What is confirmed as fact is "dodgeball had the most both times".
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The two results differ only because of the 4 who changed. The other 20 are the same, so the two results are very alike
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You worked out where the difference between the two votes came from, in numbers of people.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 4 people changed, so both results are useless
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: 20 people stayed the same, so throwing everything out because of a difference of 4 is too much.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: If you put the 4 who changed back to dodgeball, it's 14, so the first day's result is the real feeling
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You can't know whether the 4 raised their hands out of worry about others or changed their minds in a day. There's no basis to decide the first day is real.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Dodgeball had the most both times, and whether it goes over half (12) depends on the feelings of the 4 who changed
z-m-11-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You found that how many of the 4 who changed get added to dodgeball's 10 decides the 12 standard.
z-m-11-04.s.s1.reflect: At first, did you think you could say anything? How did the slip result and the story of the 4 who changed their minds change the range of what you say? Why is the phrase "in this vote" needed?
z-m-11-04.s.s2.prompt: Write one or two sentences for the class newspaper reporting the result of deciding the game. Include which voting method was used and the numbers, and write it so that how far you can say shows.
z-m-11-04.s.s2.hint.0: Decide which vote's numbers to write, and first write what method that vote used.
z-m-11-04.s.s2.hint.1: Divide the two votes into the parts where the results were the same and the parts where they were different, and write only the same parts in a confident way.
z-m-11-04.s.s2.placeholder: e.g., In the show of hands, ...
z-m-11-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: In your sentence, did you tell apart 'fact' (the numbers from the vote) and 'guess' (the real feelings)?
z-m-11-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Does your answer show which of the two methods' results you used as evidence, and why?
z-m-11-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you adjust the range of what you say without using absolute words like 'all' or 'definitely'?
z-m-11-04.s.s2.model.0: In the show of hands, dodgeball got 14 of 24, but in the slip vote without names, it was dodgeball 10, board games 8, and jump rope 6. Dodgeball had the most both times, but whether it goes over half depends on the method, so it is hard to say.
z-m-11-04.s.s2.model.1: In the slip vote, where people care less about others' eyes, dodgeball was chosen a bit more, with dodgeball 10, board games 8, and jump rope 6. So next week we will play dodgeball, and the week after that, board games.
z-m-11-04.s.s2.modelNote.1: It stated the method and used only the slip result as evidence, reflecting that the difference is not big.

z-m-11-05.title: How many boxes of snacks should we prepare for the book festival?
z-m-11-05.topic: Deciding the amount to prepare by looking at past data (a decision with several possible answers)
z-m-11-05.goal: Decide the number of boxes to prepare using the data from the past five events as evidence, understand that there are several answers that fit the conditions, and say the reason and the risk of your own choice.
z-m-11-05.material:
At the school book festival, a snack is given to each family member who comes. The numbers of people (people) who came to the past five events are as follows.

| Event | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | 5th |
| People who came | 32 | 41 | 36 | 44 | 38 |

A box has 6 snacks, and snacks can only be bought by the box (you can't buy single ones). Each person gets 1 snack. You don't know yet how many people will come to the next event.
z-m-11-05.thinking.0: Guessing the range from the biggest and smallest values of the data
z-m-11-05.thinking.1: Finding several answers that satisfy the conditions
z-m-11-05.thinking.2: Talking about the risks and benefits of a choice
z-m-11-05.prereq.0: Comparing sizes of numbers and finding the biggest and smallest number
z-m-11-05.prereq.1: Counting how many snacks there are in all when there are several boxes of 6 (Grades 3-4 level)
z-m-11-05.s.s1.prompt: About how many people will come to the next event, which statement can be said most fittingly from the data of the past five events?
z-m-11-05.s.s1.hint.0: First find the smallest number and the biggest number among the five numbers.
z-m-11-05.s.s1.hint.1: Sort out whether each choice is 'something you can actually know from the data' or 'something added that isn't in the data'.
z-m-11-05.s.s1.o.a: The past five events were between 32 and 44 people, so the next will be similar, but it could go outside that
z-m-11-05.s.s1.r.a: You guessed based on the range but left open the chance of going outside it.
z-m-11-05.s.s1.o.b: The most recent, the 5th, had 38 people, so 38 will come next time too, because it is the newest value
z-m-11-05.s.s1.r.b: You took only the value of the last time. Also look at the fact that the five numbers were different from each other.
z-m-11-05.s.s1.o.c: 44 was the most of the past five, so it will be hard for more than that to come next time
z-m-11-05.s.s1.r.c: You thought the biggest value in the past five is a limit for the future. More could come at a new event.
z-m-11-05.s.s1.o.d: The five numbers were all different, so it seems hard to guess how many will come next
z-m-11-05.s.s1.r.d: Even if the numbers are different, there is a clue that they were between 32 and 44. Saying you can't guess at all throws away the data.
z-m-11-05.s.s1.explain: The data from the five events doesn't tell you the exact number for the next event, but it shows a certain range. Base it on that range, but also think that it could go outside.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.prompt: Find 2 different numbers of boxes that satisfy all these conditions and write them. (Conditions: it must not fall short even for the day with the most people in the past five events, and the leftover snacks must be 10 or fewer.)
z-m-11-05.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a number of boxes, find how many snacks that is in all, and check whether it falls short or has leftovers when 44 people come.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.hint.1: Find the smallest number of boxes that doesn't fall short, and then see whether buying one more box still leaves no more than 10 leftovers.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of boxes is a natural number.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of boxes must be a natural number that is 1 or more.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.ok.c2: It does not fall short even on the day with the most people in the past five events (44).
z-m-11-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The snacks are fewer than 44, so it falls short on the day with the most people in the past five events.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.ok.c3: When 44 people come, the leftover snacks are 10 or fewer.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.fail.c3: When 44 people come, the leftover snacks are more than 10.
z-m-11-05.s.s2.explain: 8 boxes are 48 snacks, with 4 left over, and 9 boxes are 54, with 10 left over. 7 boxes are 42, so on a day when 44 people come, 2 are missing, and 10 boxes are 60, with 16 left over.
z-m-11-05.s.s3.prompt: How many boxes would you buy if you were really preparing? You can choose 7 boxes, not the 8 or 9 boxes found above. Write the number of boxes you chose and the reason (the risk of falling short, the leftover amount), including numbers.
z-m-11-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write how many snacks there are in all with the number of boxes you chose, and count how many days among the past five events had more people than that number.
z-m-11-05.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what happens when there aren't enough and when there are leftovers, and say which is more troublesome.
z-m-11-05.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., I would buy ... boxes. Because ...
z-m-11-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate the number of snacks for the number of boxes you chose and compare it with the numbers of people in the past five events?
z-m-11-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say which you worry about more, the risk of falling short or the leftover amount?
z-m-11-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about the case where more people come next time?
z-m-11-05.s.s3.model.0: I would buy 8 boxes (48 snacks). It's enough even for 44 people, the most in the past five events, and only 4 are left over, so there's little waste.
z-m-11-05.s.s3.model.1: I would buy 9 boxes (54 snacks). This time more than 44 might come, so I want to leave some room so we don't fall short. If any are left, we can use them at the next gathering.
z-m-11-05.s.s3.model.2: I think 7 boxes (42 snacks) is okay too. Of the past five events, only the one time 44 came would have been 2 short. If there's a way to get a few more snacks when we fall short, it's better to cut down on waste.
z-m-11-05.s.s3.modelNote.2: It breaks the condition (not falling short), but it knew the risk and even said a backup plan.

z-m-11-06.title: The same 20 students, different tables: who read it correctly?
z-m-11-06.topic: Choosing intervals when grouping data into intervals for a table
z-m-11-06.goal: Check that even with the same data, dividing the intervals differently can change which interval has the most, judge each of the two claims that read the two tables, and say how to reduce misunderstanding.
z-m-11-06.material:
The number of books (books) that 20 Grade 4 students read last month is below. (Arranged from smallest to biggest.)

0, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 5, 5, 7, 7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 9, 10

'3 to 5 books' includes 3, 4, and 5 books. Jia made Table A, grouping by 3 books, and Minho made Table B, grouping by 4 books.

Table A (grouped by 3 books)
| Interval | 0 to 2 books | 3 to 5 books | 6 to 8 books | 9 to 11 books |
| Students (number) | 3 | 7 | 8 | 2 |

Table B (grouped by 4 books)
| Interval | 0 to 3 books | 4 to 7 books | 8 to 11 books |
| Students (number) | 8 | 5 | 7 |

Jia said, "The most students read 6 to 8 books," and Minho said, "The most students read 0 to 3 books."
z-m-11-06.thinking.0: Checking both claims with the same data
z-m-11-06.thinking.1: Finding errors that arise at interval boundaries
z-m-11-06.thinking.2: Reducing misunderstanding by changing how the table is made
z-m-11-06.prereq.0: Counting data and organizing it in a table (Grades 3-4 level)
z-m-11-06.prereq.1: Understanding the meaning of an interval like '0 to 2 books' that includes both the first and last numbers
z-m-11-06.s.s1.prompt: We checked what each person said against each table and the 20 numbers above. Which judgment is correct?
z-m-11-06.s.s1.hint.0: Add up the number of students in each table and check that it is 20.
z-m-11-06.s.s1.hint.1: For each of Table A and Table B, count the 20 numbers directly to check whether the biggest box is right.
z-m-11-06.s.s1.o.a: Jia misread the big box in Table A, and Minho is right
z-m-11-06.s.s1.r.a: In Table A, 6 to 8 books is 8 students, the biggest box. Jia did not misread the table.
z-m-11-06.s.s1.o.b: Both read their own table correctly, and it looks different because the intervals are different
z-m-11-06.s.s1.r.b: You read the biggest box in each table exactly, and found that how you divide the intervals can change the story.
z-m-11-06.s.s1.o.c: The two tables don't seem to count all 20 students, so both are wrong
z-m-11-06.s.s1.r.c: Add up the number of students in each table. Both tables total 20.
z-m-11-06.s.s1.o.d: Minho misread the big box in Table B, and Jia is right
z-m-11-06.s.s1.r.d: In Table B, 0 to 3 books is 8 students, the biggest box. Minho did not misread the table either.
z-m-11-06.s.s1.explain: In Table A, 6 to 8 books is the biggest with 8 students, and in Table B, 0 to 3 books is the biggest with 8 students. Both tables total 20 students. Nobody misread a table; the 'interval with the most' changed depending on how the intervals were divided.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.prompt: Seonyeong compared the two tables and summed it up as below. Which line is strange? (Line numbers start from 1.)
z-m-11-06.s.s2.hint.0: From the 20 numbers, pick out and write all the numbers of books of the students who go in the 3 to 5 books box of Table A.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.hint.1: Check one by one whether the numbers you picked all fall in the 4 to 7 books interval of Table B.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.line.0: 1. Table A is 3, 7, 8, and 2 students, and adding them all gives 20 students.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.line.1: 2. Table B is 8, 5, and 7 students, and adding them all gives 20 students.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.line.2: 3. Both tables counted all 20 students, so only how the intervals were grouped is different.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.line.3: 4. The 3 to 5 books box of Table A is 7 students, and all 7 of these go in the 4 to 7 books box of Table B, so the 4 to 7 books box of Table B must be 7 or more.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.line.4: 5. In Table B, students who read 3 books go in the 0 to 3 books box, so the 0 to 3 books box of Table B looks bigger than in Table A.
z-m-11-06.s.s2.explain: Line 4 is strange. The 3 to 5 books box of Table A includes 5 students who read 3 books, and 3 books goes into the 0 to 3 books box in Table B. So the 4 to 7 books box of Table B is 5 students, not 7 or more. You missed that which box a value on the boundary of an interval goes into is different in each table.
z-m-11-06.s.s3.prompt: You want to put 'the books our class read in a month' in the class newspaper as a table. Write how to decide the intervals and what to show along with it so that misunderstanding is reduced.
z-m-11-06.s.s3.hint.0: First write in one sentence why Jia's and Minho's statements looked different from each other.
z-m-11-06.s.s3.hint.1: To keep that from happening again, write one thing each that a newspaper reader should know and be able to see.
z-m-11-06.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., I would set the intervals ...
z-m-11-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your method reduce the case where things look different from each other, like Jia's and Minho's statements?
z-m-11-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you think of an example like Table A and Table B and test your method with it?
z-m-11-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Besides intervals, did you think about showing the 20 numbers themselves too (like a bar graph counted one by one)?
z-m-11-06.s.s3.model.0: I would write in the article how I divided the intervals, and also show a table divided with other intervals. If I also print a bar graph that counts the number of books read one by one, as 1 book, 2 books, ..., I think misunderstanding caused by intervals would go down.
z-m-11-06.s.s3.model.1: If you group with only one kind of interval, the story can change, so I would check with two different interval sizes, and write in the newspaper only the statements that come out the same in both tables.
z-m-11-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: It is a method of not deciding a conclusion from one interval, and writing only statements that hold in both tables.

z-m-11-07.title: Remaking the choices on a book survey so they don't overlap
z-m-11-07.topic: Making survey items (choices): no overlaps and nothing left out
z-m-11-07.goal: Think through how to read the results when the choices on a survey overlap or leave things out, and make choices yourself that don't overlap and that let everyone choose one.
z-m-11-07.material:
Class 3 of Grade 4 surveyed 'the kind of book they want to read' to buy new books for the class library. Each person chose only one, and all 27 students answered. The choices on the survey and the results are as follows.

| Choice | Fairy tale books | Comic books | Biographies | Story books | Science books |
| Students (number of people) | 8 | 9 | 3 | 5 | 2 |

(The survey said that fairy tale books are books with imaginary stories, and story books are books with a plot. History books and poetry books were not among the choices.)
z-m-11-07.thinking.0: Finding the problems in the survey design
z-m-11-07.thinking.1: Working out how overlap affects reading the results
z-m-11-07.thinking.2: Making choices yourself and giving the reason
z-m-11-07.prereq.0: Reading survey results organized in a table
z-m-11-07.prereq.1: Knowing the difference between 'choosing only one' and 'choosing several'
z-m-11-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the problems that can come from the choices on this survey.
z-m-11-07.s.s1.hint.0: Think of one book that fits both fairy tale books and story books. Which one do you think a student would choose?
z-m-11-07.s.s1.hint.1: Think of a few more kinds of books people want to read, and look at whether any don't fit anywhere in the choices.
z-m-11-07.s.s1.o.a: There are 5 choices, so it's hard for students to choose only one
z-m-11-07.s.s1.r.a: 5 is not many. The problem is not the number but the relationship between the choices.
z-m-11-07.s.s1.o.b: Fairy tale books and story books overlap, so the box students choose can differ from student to student
z-m-11-07.s.s1.r.b: You found that the two choices are similar, so people may choose differently for the same book.
z-m-11-07.s.s1.o.c: Comic books are among the choices, so the survey becomes incorrect
z-m-11-07.s.s1.r.c: A book being among the choices doesn't make the survey wrong. Think about whether the choices overlap or leave something out.
z-m-11-07.s.s1.o.d: A student who wants to read history books or poetry books has no choice to pick
z-m-11-07.s.s1.r.d: You found that there are students who want a kind that isn't on the survey. They answered, but they may not be able to put in their own thoughts.
z-m-11-07.s.s1.explain: If the choices overlap, students with the same thought can go into different boxes, and if some kinds are missing, those students have to force themselves to choose the nearest box. A large number of choices or a certain kind being included is not a problem.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.prompt: Junho spoke as below after seeing the survey results. Which line is strange? (Line numbers start from 1.)
z-m-11-07.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether, among the 5 students who chose story books, there could be students who also like fairy tale books.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.hint.1: In each line, check 'whether the same student could go in twice when you add or compare boxes'.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.line.0: 1. Each person chose only one, so 27, the sum of all the numbers in the table, is the number of students who answered.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.line.1: 2. Comic books, with 9 students, is the box chosen the most.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.line.2: 3. The 3 for biographies and the 2 for science books are different students, so together they are 5.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.line.3: 4. 8 students chose fairy tale books, so only 8 students like fairy tale books.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.line.4: 5. The students who chose comic books are 1 more than the students who chose fairy tale books.
z-m-11-07.s.s2.explain: Line 4 is strange. Among the 5 students who chose story books, there may also be students who like fairy tale books, so more than 8 students may like fairy tale books. Since each person chose only one, you can combine boxes as in lines 1 and 3.
z-m-11-07.s.s3.prompt: Remake the choices on the survey. Write 5 or fewer, make them so they don't overlap so that each person chooses only one, and make sure there is a place for every student to choose. Then write the reason you divided them that way in one or two sentences.
z-m-11-07.s.s3.hint.0: First decide one standard for dividing books (for example, content or shape), and write the choices by that standard.
z-m-11-07.s.s3.hint.1: Think of three book titles and test one by one whether each goes into exactly one of the choices.
z-m-11-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you test with examples whether there is a book that fits two or more of your choices at the same time?
z-m-11-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is there a place for a student who wants to read history books or poetry books to choose?
z-m-11-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: If you added a box like 'other books', did you think about whether that box might become too big?
z-m-11-07.s.s3.model.0: Choices: story books (including fairy tale books), comic books, science books, history and biographies, other books. Fairy tale books and story books overlap, so I combined them into one, and I added 'other books' so that students who want to read books that fit nowhere can choose it.
z-m-11-07.s.s3.model.1: Choices: novels, comic books, knowledge books (science and history), poetry books, biographies. I divided them by the content of the books so that a book doesn't straddle two boxes. Since no boxes overlap, I think students will end up choosing the same box.
z-m-11-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: It divided by a content standard and checked that they don't overlap, but it didn't talk about 'leaving out'.

z-m-11-08.title: A day where the start and end are the same: can we say there was no change?
z-m-11-08.topic: Reading the changes in the middle of a line graph when the start and end are the same
z-m-11-08.goal: Make a counterexample showing that even when the start and end values are the same, it may have changed in the middle, and tell apart what can and can't be known from the graph.
z-m-11-08.material:
The temperature of the playground was measured every 3 hours and shown in a line graph. (There is no picture. The values of the points are as follows.)

| Time | 9 a.m. | 12 noon | 3 p.m. | 6 p.m. |
| Temperature (℃) | 14 | 19 | 21 | 14 |

Minjun said, "The temperature at 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. is the same, 14℃, so the playground temperature didn't change all day that day."
z-m-11-08.thinking.0: Testing a claim with a counterexample
z-m-11-08.thinking.1: Making several examples that satisfy the conditions
z-m-11-08.thinking.2: Telling apart what can and can't be known from the graph
z-m-11-08.prereq.0: Reading points and values on a line graph (Grade 4 level)
z-m-11-08.prereq.1: Finding the difference between a big number and a small number
z-m-11-08.s.s1.prompt: What can you say from this graph about Minjun's statement?
z-m-11-08.s.s1.hint.0: Read the values of the four points of the graph in order and write them down.
z-m-11-08.s.s1.hint.1: Look at whether the same value as the starting value is also in the middle.
z-m-11-08.s.s1.o.a: The start and end are the same, so the temperature in between must have been the same all the time
z-m-11-08.s.s1.r.a: You guessed that the middle would be the same just by looking at the start and end. Actually read the values of the middle points.
z-m-11-08.s.s1.o.b: The two middle points being higher than 14℃ must be a measuring mistake
z-m-11-08.s.s1.r.b: You threw away the values because the middle points are different. There is no evidence anywhere that they were measured wrongly.
z-m-11-08.s.s1.o.c: The two middle points are higher than 14℃, so you can't say it didn't change
z-m-11-08.s.s1.r.c: You judged by reading the middle points together, not only the start and end.
z-m-11-08.s.s1.o.d: It was measured every 3 hours, so you can't know the temperature at any time
z-m-11-08.s.s1.r.d: You can read the values at the times measured (9, 12, 3, 6) from the graph. Saying you can't know anything is too much.
z-m-11-08.s.s1.explain: If you read all four points of the graph, they are 14, 19, 21, 14℃. Even though the start and end are the same, it rose by as much as 7℃ in the middle and came back down, so the statement 'it didn't change' is not right.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 other days in which Minjun's statement is wrong. Write the temperatures (℃, whole numbers) at 9 a.m., 12 noon, 3 p.m., and 6 p.m. in order as t1, t2, t3, t4. (Conditions: the temperatures at 9 and 6 are the same; the difference between the highest and lowest of the four values is 5℃ or more; the difference between two neighboring measurements is 8℃ or less; and all values are from 0℃ to 35℃. If the pair of the 12 noon and 3 p.m. temperatures is different, it counts as a different example.)
z-m-11-08.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the temperatures at 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. as the same value.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.hint.1: Decide the values of the two middle times as higher (or lower) than the starting value, and check whether the difference between the highest and lowest values is 5 or more.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.ok.c1: All temperatures are whole numbers from 0℃ to 35℃.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.fail.c1: All temperatures must be whole numbers from 0 to 35.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The temperatures at 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. are the same.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The temperatures at 9 a.m. (t1) and 6 p.m. (t4) must be the same.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.ok.c3: The difference between the highest and lowest values is 5℃ or more, so the temperature changed during the day.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The difference between the highest and lowest values is less than 5℃, so it becomes a day with almost no change.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.ok.c4: The difference between two neighboring measurements is 8℃ or less.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.fail.c4: Changing by more than 8℃ in 3 hours is too sudden.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.explain: Days like (14, 19, 21, 14), where the start and end are the same but the middle goes up, or (20, 13, 12, 20), which goes down and comes back up, are possible. (14, 14, 14, 14) is a day that really didn't change, so it can't be a counterexample, and (10, 25, 25, 10) changes by 15℃ in 3 hours, which is too sudden.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.prompt: Pick one example you made, and write with numbers what you can't tell from 'the temperatures at 9 and 6 are the same' alone and can only tell by looking at the middle values.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: In the four values you made, cover the start and end and think about what you can tell from just the two middle values.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write side by side the statement you guessed by looking only at the start and end and the statement you learned by looking at all four points.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Can the 'things you can know' that you mentioned really be read from the four values you made?
z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: For times that weren't measured (for example, 10 a.m.), what did you say you don't know?

z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.model.0: My example is 14, 19, 21, 14℃. Even though 9 and 6 are the same at 14℃, it was 19℃ at 12 and 21℃ at 3, so you can tell the temperature rose in the daytime and came back down. If you look at only the start and end, you don't know this.
z-m-11-08.s.s2.because.model.1: Even if the start and end are the same, the middle values can be different. In my 12, 15, 17, 12, 9 and 6 are the same at 12℃, but it rose to 17℃ at 3 p.m. But I can't tell from this graph what it was like at 10, between 9 and 12.
